subtitle: Look at any DSD decision in terms of where its effects land and who must travel farther for less. You will learn to name those gaps and fix the default before it locks in.
scope: For DSD leaders, supervisors and policy, rates, contracts and data staff who shape programs that reach rural, suburban, urban and Tribal communities, and for anyone who wants shared language about place. It is not a substitute for Tribal consultation under state law, formal rate or contract decisions, or the equity analysis process itself.
introTranscript: Welcome. This course is about place. A waiver service that works in Hennepin County may not exist within a two-hour drive in the northwest. A rate that covers travel in a suburb may not cover it on a reservation. The same portal, the same policy, the same rate, land differently depending on where a person lives. Over six lessons you will learn the plain words for geographic equity, see how it shows up in DSD work, look at who carries the cost when the default stands, learn a short method for reading any decision by place, practice harder calls, and apply it to one piece of live work. The course is voluntary. It does not score you or anyone else.

lessons.title: Place Is a Variable, Not a Footnote
lessons.summary: Geographic equity means the same policy produces fair access in every part of Minnesota, not identical treatment.
lessons.objective: Define geographic equity and name the four settings in plain words.
takeaways: Identical treatment across counties is not the same as equal access.
Rural, suburban, urban and Tribal are four different access conditions, not one spectrum.
Tribal Nations are governments, and place questions there also carry a consultation duty.
lessons.statement: The default: a statewide policy is written once and assumed to land the same everywhere. The better practice: every policy, rate and timeline is read for how it lands in each of the four settings before it is final.

image.caption: A main street in greater Minnesota, where the same statewide portal does not reach the same way it does in a metro suburb.

intro.heading: What geographic equity means here
intro.body:
Geographic equity is a simple test. Does a person with the same need get a comparable chance at services whether they live in a metro suburb, a city neighborhood, a farm township or on Tribal land? Not an identical service. A comparable chance. The Olmstead Plan commits Minnesota to community living in the most integrated setting, and that promise only holds if the setting is reachable from where someone actually lives.

The four settings in this course are rural, suburban, urban and Tribal. They are not points on a line from less to more. Each has its own access conditions. Rural areas often have few providers, long drives and thin broadband. Suburbs may have providers but gaps in transit and in language access. Urban areas may have many providers and still have waits, high turnover and neighborhoods that providers avoid. Tribal areas carry all of these plus a legal fact: Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and the state has a consultation duty under Minnesota law whenever a DHS decision affects them.

In DSD work the place variable hides inside ordinary objects. A rate. A travel reimbursement rule. A provider enrollment form. A training that is only offered in person in St. Paul. This lesson gives you the words. The rest of the course shows you where to look.

inThisLesson: Define geographic equity in one sentence you can use in a meeting.
Distinguish the four settings and the access conditions of each.
Learn five terms that recur across DSD policy, rates and contracting.
Try a knowledge check and a sort on everyday DSD objects.
lessons.keyStatement: A policy that is the same everywhere is not fair everywhere until someone checks where it lands.

flashcards.back: People with comparable needs have a comparable chance at services regardless of where in Minnesota they live.
An area where an authorized service exists on paper but no enrolled provider is available within a reasonable distance or wait.
The county, Tribal Nation or managed care organization responsible for assessing eligibility and coordinating waiver services for a person.
A government-to-government process required by Minnesota law when a state agency action affects Tribal Nations; it is a formal duty, not a courtesy.
The time, cost and risk a person or worker absorbs to reach a service; it is often invisible in a rate or a timeline.

items.title: Rural
items.body: Few enrolled providers, long distances, limited transit and uneven broadband. A service that is authorized may have no one to deliver it.

items.title: Suburban
items.body: Providers exist but may cluster near highways. Transit gaps, language access and affordable housing shape who can actually use them.

items.title: Urban
items.body: Many providers and still long waits. High staff turnover, neighborhoods providers avoid, and capacity that does not match need by language or culture.

items.title: Tribal
items.body: Often rural conditions plus jurisdiction questions, Tribal programs that are their own systems, and a formal consultation duty for the state.

tabs.label: Rates
tabs.body: A rate built on an average travel time pays a metro provider well and a rural one poorly. The rate is identical. The margin is not.

tabs.label: Timelines
tabs.body: A thirty-day implementation window assumes staff can be trained quickly. In a county with two case managers, thirty days is a different number.

tabs.label: Forms and portals
tabs.body: An online-only form assumes broadband and a device. In parts of the state that assumption fails for people and for small providers.

tabs.label: Meetings
tabs.body: An in-person listening session in the metro hears from the metro. Everyone else is represented by whoever could afford the drive.

check.question: A DSD unit publishes a new provider training as a single in-person session in St. Paul. A rural lead agency asks why their providers were left out. Which description of the situation is most accurate?
check.correct: The training was offered identically to everyone, but access was not equal because travel burden was not considered.
wrong: Access was equal because every provider was invited to the same session.
The rural agency should arrange its own training since location is a local matter.
There is no geographic issue because the content applies statewide.
check.feedbackCorrect: Identical offer, unequal access. Naming that difference is the first skill in this course.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Look at who had to travel and what that cost them. The offer was the same; the chance to use it was not.

items.text: The nearest enrolled day service is ninety minutes away by car.
Three providers serve the neighborhood but each has a six-month wait.
The Nation runs its own health program and asks how the new waiver rule fits it.
Broadband drops out during the remote assessment.
The state must consult before the rate change takes effect in the area.
Staff turnover means the person has had four support workers this year.

lessons.next: Next, look at how these conditions show up in the everyday objects of DSD work: rates, enrollment, timelines and meetings.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Morgan leads a policy unit drafting guidance for a new HCBS service. The draft says providers must complete an online module and attend a quarterly in-person meeting in the metro. A colleague from a northern county reads it and says, quietly, that none of their three providers will do this. Morgan has a week before the guidance is final and believes the content is sound. The team has not yet asked anyone outside the metro to review it.
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful first move for Morgan?
options: Pull the draft for a short place review: list the four settings and ask how each requirement lands in each one before finalizing.
Keep the draft as written since the content is correct, and add a note that exceptions can be requested.
Remove the in-person requirement entirely so no one has to travel.
responses: This is the practice. A short, structured read by setting usually finds two or three fixes without losing the content.
Exceptions put the burden on the people with the least capacity to ask. The default still stands for everyone who does not.
This may be right, but deciding it before looking at all four settings skips the step that would tell you. Some meetings matter; the question is where and how.

lessons.transfer: Think of one statewide rule, form or meeting you touched this month. Without naming anyone, where in Minnesota would it have been hardest to comply with, and what would that person have had to absorb to do it?

move.control: You control whether a draft you own gets a read by setting before it moves to sign-off.
move.failure: The guidance goes out statewide, the metro complies, and the first signal from elsewhere is a complaint six months later.
move.next: This week, the draft owner adds a one-line place note to the cover memo of one active document and reviews it with their supervisor by Friday.

lessons.title: Where the Metro Default Lives
lessons.summary: Most DSD defaults were written from the metro and travel outward with their assumptions intact.
lessons.objective: Identify the common metro default in a rate, timeline, enrollment rule or engagement plan.
takeaways: The default is usually not a decision; it is an assumption no one wrote down.
Travel, broadband, provider count and transit are the four assumptions that fail most often.
A map of enrolled providers tells you more than a list of authorized services.
lessons.statement: The default: a decision is drafted where most staff sit and tested against the providers they know. The better practice: the draft is tested against the county with the fewest providers and the Nation whose programs it touches.

image.caption: A waiting area in Minnesota; how long people sit here depends heavily on which part of the state they live in.

intro.heading: Defaults travel; conditions do not
intro.body:
Most DSD policy is written in St. Paul by people who commute to it. That is not a fault. It is a fact about where assumptions come from. When a drafter pictures a provider, they picture the ones they have met. When they picture a drive, they picture theirs. The draft carries those pictures into every county and onto every reservation, where the conditions are different and the pictures are wrong.

Four assumptions fail most often. Travel: a rule that requires in-person visits at a set frequency costs a rural worker a day per visit. Broadband: an online portal, a remote assessment or a video training assumes a connection that is not always there for people or small providers. Provider count: a choice requirement assumes there is more than one provider to choose from. Transit: a community integration goal assumes the person can get to the community.

The tell is often a single sentence in a policy that reads as neutral. 'Providers must respond within two business days.' 'Members may select from the enrolled provider list.' 'Training will be offered in person.' None of these name a place. All of them land differently by place. This lesson teaches you to spot that sentence, so you can bring it to the right table before it is final.

inThisLesson: Name the four assumptions that most often fail outside the metro.
Read three neutral-sounding policy sentences for their hidden place.
Compare an authorized service list with an enrolled provider map.
Practice a scenario where the default is already written.
lessons.keyStatement: The sentence that names no place is the one to read twice.

items.title: Travel is short
items.body: Visit frequency, in-person requirements and mileage caps are set with metro distances in mind. Elsewhere they consume whole days.

items.title: Broadband is there
items.body: Online-only forms, portals and remote assessments assume a stable connection and a device. Parts of greater Minnesota and some Tribal areas do not have that.

items.title: There is a choice
items.body: Person-centered planning assumes a list of options. In a provider desert the list has one name or none.

items.title: Transit exists
items.body: Community integration, employment and day services all assume the person can get there. Without transit, the goal is a sentence in a plan.

tabs.label: Respond in two days
tabs.body: A metro agency with a dozen staff absorbs this. A rural 245D provider with one administrator who also drives shifts does not. The rule is neutral; the burden is not.

tabs.label: Select from the list
tabs.body: Choice is real where the list is long. Where it has one name, the person is choosing between that provider and nothing, and the plan still records a choice.

tabs.label: Offered in person
tabs.body: Offered where? A single location is a decision about who attends. Hybrid and recorded options change who the training reaches.

check.question: A rates team proposes a mileage cap for in-home services that matches the current metro average. Which of these is the most likely effect?
check.correct: Rural and Tribal area providers absorb unpaid travel, and some stop accepting distant clients.
wrong: The cap affects all providers equally because it is the same number for everyone.
Rural providers will bill more visits to make up the difference.
The cap has no effect because providers can already choose their service area.
check.feedbackCorrect: A single number lands unevenly. Providers respond to margin, and distant clients lose service without any policy saying so.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Ask what the number pays for in each setting. The same cap covers a metro drive and leaves a rural one unpaid.

items.text: Monthly in-person visits are required for every waiver participant.
Enrollment is accepted only through the online portal.
The person-centered plan lists one option because one exists.
Remote assessments freeze and restart in two counties.
The worker spends a full day for a one-hour visit.
A person leaves a provider and has no one to move to.

lessons.next: Next, turn to who carries the cost when these defaults stand, and what Minnesota policy already says about it.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jordan supervises a contracts unit preparing a new provider agreement. The draft includes a two-business-day response standard and an online-only incident submission form. Jordan's team has reviewed it with three metro providers who found it reasonable. A Tribal human services director on the stakeholder list has not responded. The agreement is due to procurement in ten days, and Jordan is being asked whether it is ready.
scenario.prompt: What should Jordan do before saying it is ready?
options: Say it is ready, since three providers reviewed it and the Tribal director had the same chance to respond.
Hold it, reach the Tribal director and at least one rural provider directly, and read the two standards against their conditions.
Remove the response standard and the online form so there is nothing to object to.
responses: Three metro readers tested the draft against metro conditions. A non-response is not feedback, and where a Tribal Nation is affected it may also be a consultation question.

Yes. Ten days is enough to reach two more readers and adjust two standards. Where the Nation's programs are affected, route the question to the Tribal consultation process rather than treating it as feedback.
Dropping standards is not the same as testing them. Some version of both may be needed; the question is how they land, not whether they exist.

lessons.transfer: Recall a document you reviewed recently that read as neutral. Which sentence in it would have cost the most to comply with in the county with the fewest providers, and who would have paid that cost?

move.control: You control which readers see a draft and whether the reader list includes someone outside the metro.
move.failure: Review lists stay the same, every draft tests well, and the gaps appear only in complaints and missed authorizations.
move.next: By the end of next week, the unit lead adds one rural and one Tribal area reader to the standing list for one document type and confirms it with the team.

lessons.title: Who Travels Farther for Less
lessons.summary: When the place default stands, the cost lands on specific people and communities, and Minnesota policy already names the duty.
lessons.objective: Describe who carries the burden of a geographic default and cite the policy that applies.
takeaways: People in provider deserts pay in waits, distance and fewer choices; workers pay in unpaid time.
The Olmstead Plan, the DHS Equity Policy and the Tribal consultation statute all speak to place.
Good practice means data by county and Tribal area, not statewide averages.
lessons.statement: The default: statewide numbers look fine and the policy is judged a success. The better practice: results are read by county and by Tribal area, and the places that fell behind get named and resourced.

image.caption: Printed pages on a desk; a statewide average can hide the counties and Nations that are not being reached.

intro.heading: The cost has an address
intro.body:
When a geographic default stands, the cost is not spread evenly. It concentrates. A person on a waiver in a county with one enrolled provider waits longer, travels farther and often accepts a service that is not the one they wanted. A direct support worker in that county drives unpaid miles or leaves the field. A Tribal member may face a state system and a Tribal system that do not talk to each other. A family in a suburb without transit watches a community goal stay on paper. None of these appear in a statewide average.

Minnesota policy already names the duty. The Olmstead Plan commits the state to integrated community living, which requires services to be reachable. The DHS Equity Policy asks that decisions be examined for differential impact, and place is one of the dimensions on which impact differs. Minnesota Statutes 10.65 requires state agencies to consult with Tribal Nations on actions that affect them. The HCBS settings rule from CMS expects community settings to offer real access to the community, which is a place question by definition.

Good practice is not complicated. Count providers by county and by Tribal area. Read wait times and authorizations the same way. When a place falls behind, say so in the report and say what will be done. Averages are a way of not seeing.

inThisLesson: Trace who absorbs the cost of a place default in a waiver service.
Connect the Olmstead Plan, the DHS Equity Policy and the consultation statute to place.
Compare a statewide average with a county view of the same measure.
Decide what good practice looks like in a data report.
lessons.keyStatement: A statewide average is a decision not to look at the places that fell behind.

items.title: Olmstead Plan
items.body: Minnesota's plan commits to community living in the most integrated setting. A setting that cannot be reached is not integrated for the person who cannot reach it.

items.title: DHS Equity Policy
items.body: The policy asks units to look at how decisions affect different communities. Geography is one of those differences, alongside race, disability, language and culture.

items.title: Tribal consultation statute
items.body: Minnesota Statutes 10.65 requires state agencies to consult with Tribal Nations on actions with Tribal implications. It is a government-to-government duty, not a stakeholder step.

items.title: HCBS settings rule
items.body: Federal rules expect waiver settings to give people real access to the community. Whether that is true depends on where the setting is and what is around it.

tabs.heading: Who pays when the default stands

tabs.label: The person
tabs.body: Longer waits, longer drives, fewer real choices, and goals that remain in the plan because the thing they describe is not nearby.

tabs.label: The worker
tabs.body: Unpaid travel, split shifts across long distances, and turnover that leaves one person serving a whole township.

tabs.label: The Nation
tabs.body: A state decision that does not fit Tribal programs, made without consultation, which the Nation then has to work around.

tabs.label: The lead agency
tabs.body: Authorizations that cannot be filled, complaints about waits, and reporting that looks like local failure when the cause is statewide design.

check.question: A quarterly report shows statewide authorization-to-service time within target. A supervisor in a northwestern county says their people are waiting far longer. What is the best response from the data team?
check.correct: Break the measure out by county and Tribal area and report the places outside target alongside the statewide figure.
wrong: Explain that the statewide figure is the official measure and local variation is expected.
Ask the county to submit its own data separately since it has a concern.
Note the concern and revisit it if the statewide figure moves out of target.
check.feedbackCorrect: Disaggregating by place is the practice. The statewide figure is not wrong, but it is not the whole report.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The supervisor is describing something the average hides. Looking by county and Tribal area shows whether the target is met everywhere or only on balance.

items.text: Ninety-one percent of authorizations filled within target.
Eight counties and two Tribal areas below target, listed by name.
Rates unit to review the travel component for the listed areas by next quarter.
Median wait for day services, statewide.
Enrolled providers per thousand waiver participants, by county.
Consultation requested with the two affected Nations before the rule is final.

lessons.next: Next, you get the method: a short place read you can run on any decision in under an hour.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Avery manages a data and evaluation team asked to summarize the first year of a new waiver service for leadership. The statewide uptake is strong. Avery's analyst mentions that three counties and one Tribal area show almost no uptake, and that the enrolled provider map for those areas is nearly empty. The leadership summary is one page. Avery's director prefers a clean story and has asked for the headline number.
scenario.prompt: How should Avery frame the one-page summary?
options: Lead with the statewide number and keep the place detail in an appendix for anyone who asks.
Lead with the place gaps and leave the statewide number out, since it is misleading.
Report the statewide number and, in the same paragraph, name the areas with no uptake and the provider gap that explains it, with a proposed next step.
responses: The appendix is where place gaps go to be forgotten. Leadership reads the page, not the attachment.
The statewide number is real and useful. Dropping it trades one incomplete story for another.
This is the practice. Both facts on the same page, the cause named, and an owner for the next step. The clean story is the true one.

lessons.transfer: Think of one measure your unit reports regularly. If it were broken out by county and Tribal area tomorrow, which places do you suspect would fall behind, and what would you want the report to say about them?

move.control: You control whether a report you own shows results by place, or only on balance.
move.failure: Reports stay statewide, leadership hears success, and the counties and Nations that fell behind keep falling behind quietly.
move.next: The report owner adds a by-place breakout to one recurring measure before the next cycle and reviews it with the data lead on the next team date.

lessons.title: The One-Hour Place Read
lessons.summary: A four-step read that tests any decision against rural, suburban, urban and Tribal conditions before it locks.
lessons.objective: Apply the four-step place read to a draft decision and record the result.
takeaways: Map, Test, Ask, Adjust: four steps, one page, under an hour.
Test the draft against the hardest county, not the typical one.
If a Tribal Nation is affected, the Ask step routes to consultation, not to a survey.
lessons.statement: The default: the draft is reviewed for content and compliance and goes to sign-off. The better practice: the draft also gets a place read, and the one-page result travels with it to sign-off.

image.caption: A one-page worksheet and a pen; the place read fits on a single sheet and goes with the draft.

intro.heading: Map, Test, Ask, Adjust
intro.body:
The place read has four steps and fits on one page. It works on a rate, a policy memo, a contract term, a training plan, a timeline or an engagement plan. It takes under an hour.

Map. Write down which parts of Minnesota the decision touches. Name the counties with the fewest enrolled providers for this service and the Tribal Nations whose programs or members it affects. If you do not know, that is the first finding. Test. Read the draft as if you were a provider, a lead agency worker and a person on the waiver in the hardest county you named. For each requirement, ask what it costs there in travel, connection, choice and transit. Write the costs down, even rough ones.

Ask. Reach at least one person from the hardest setting and one from a Tribal area before the draft is final. If a Nation is affected, this step is not a survey. It goes to the DHS Tribal consultation process, and the draft waits for it. Adjust. Change the draft where the cost was high: add a hybrid option, a travel component, a longer window, a paper path. Record what changed and what did not and why. Attach the page to the draft.

That is the whole method. The hard part is doing it before sign-off rather than after the complaint.

inThisLesson: Walk through Map, Test, Ask and Adjust on a sample draft.
Choose the hardest county and the affected Nations for a service.
Separate what goes to consultation from what goes to ordinary review.
Record the result on one page that travels with the draft.
lessons.keyStatement: Test the draft against the hardest county, then send it to sign-off with the page attached.

items.title: Map
items.body: List the places the decision touches. Name the counties with the fewest providers for this service and the Nations affected. Not knowing is a finding.

items.title: Test
items.body: Read each requirement from the hardest county as a provider, a worker and a person. Write what it costs in travel, connection, choice and transit.

items.title: Ask
items.body: Reach one person from the hardest setting and one from a Tribal area before the draft is final. Tribal effects go to consultation, not to a feedback form.

items.title: Adjust
items.body: Change the draft where costs were high. Record what changed, what did not, and why. Attach the page.

tabs.label: Hybrid and recorded
tabs.body: Any required meeting or training gets a remote option and a recording. Where broadband is weak, a phone option or a regional in-person site.

tabs.label: Travel component
tabs.body: Rates and contracts that involve in-person work include travel time or mileage that reflects the service area, not a statewide average.

tabs.label: Longer window
tabs.body: Implementation timelines give small providers and thin counties more time, with a check-in rather than a cliff.

tabs.label: Paper path
tabs.body: Every online-only form keeps a paper or phone route. It costs little and keeps people and providers from falling out.

check.question: During the Ask step on a new rate methodology, a policy lead learns the change affects services on two reservations. What does the method say to do?
check.correct: Route the question to the DHS Tribal consultation process and hold the draft until that has happened.
wrong: Send the two Tribal human services directors the stakeholder survey with a note that their input is important.
Note the effect in the Adjust step and proceed, since the rate applies statewide.
Ask the lead agencies in those counties to pass along any concerns from the Nations.
check.feedbackCorrect: Tribal effects are a door, not a feedback item. Consultation is a government-to-government duty and the draft waits for it.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A survey or a county intermediary is not consultation. When a Nation is affected, the method routes to the formal process before the draft moves.

items.text: List the five counties with the fewest enrolled providers for this service.
Read the two-day response rule as a one-person provider in that county.
Add a phone route for the incident form.
Name the Nations whose members use this service.
Estimate the unpaid travel a monthly visit requirement creates.
Extend the implementation window and add a check-in at sixty days.

lessons.next: Next, practice harder calls and name the situations that must go through a required reporting or consultation process rather than a team discussion.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Riley coordinates an implementation timeline for a change to a 245D service standard. The plan gives all providers sixty days. Riley runs the place read and finds that in two rural counties the only providers are small, with one administrator each, and that the required training is online-only. Riley's director wants a single statewide date for simplicity. The place read page is finished and shows the cost clearly.
scenario.prompt: What should Riley bring to the director?
options: The single statewide date as requested, with a note that rural providers can ask for extensions.
The place read page, with a proposal for a statewide date plus a defined check-in and a phone training option for small providers, and a record of why.
A recommendation to delay the whole change until every provider can comply on the same day.
responses: Extensions on request shift the work to the providers least able to do it. The director gets simplicity; the counties get the cost.
This keeps the single date the director wants and adjusts the two things that failed the test. The page explains the reasoning so the decision is on record.
A statewide delay for everyone is rarely the answer. The method asks for targeted adjustments, not a stop.

lessons.transfer: Pick one draft you could run the place read on this week. Which county would you choose as the hardest test, and what is the one requirement you already suspect would fail there?

move.control: You control whether the place read page is attached to a draft before it goes to sign-off.
move.failure: The method is admired and not run, and drafts keep moving on content review alone.
move.next: The draft owner runs the read on one live draft this week and attaches the page; the supervisor reviews it at the next one-to-one.

lessons.title: Difficult Decisions and Required Consultation
lessons.summary: Some place questions are judgment calls to practice; others belong to a formal office and must go there.
lessons.objective: Distinguish place decisions you can work through from those that require a reporting or consultation process.
takeaways: Tribal effects, rate setting, procurement terms and eligibility are doors, not workshops.
Judgment calls are about how a decision lands; doors are about who has authority to decide.
Naming a door early saves time; naming it late looks like avoidance.
lessons.statement: The default: a team talks a place problem through until it feels resolved and moves on. The better practice: the team sorts the problem first, works the parts it owns, and sends the rest through the right door without delay.

image.caption: A packet on a table; when a Tribal Nation is affected, consultation is a door the packet goes through, not a bullet in it.

intro.heading: Work it or route it
intro.body:
By now you can see place in a draft. The next skill is knowing which place problems your team can work and which belong to a formal office. Getting this wrong in either direction is costly. Workshopping a consultation duty is a legal problem. Sending every judgment call to legal is a way of never deciding.

The doors in DSD work are clear. If a decision affects a Tribal Nation, its members or its programs, it goes to the DHS Tribal consultation process under Minnesota Statutes 10.65. If it changes a rate, it goes through the rates and legislative process, not a unit meeting. If it changes a contract term, procurement owns the term. If it changes who is eligible or how a lead agency assesses, that is eligibility policy with its own process. If a person or provider raises discrimination based on where they live combined with race, disability, language or another protected basis, that is the Equal Opportunity and Access Division or the Minnesota Department of Human Rights. If a place gap is creating risk of harm to a vulnerable adult, maltreatment reporting applies.

Everything else is judgment: how to phrase a requirement, where to hold a meeting, whether to add a paper path, how long a window should be. Practice those. Route the rest, and say so in the record.

inThisLesson: Identify when a place-related decision requires reporting or consultation.
Sort a set of place problems into work-it or route-it.
Practice three harder cases where the line is not obvious.
Write the one sentence that records a routing decision.
lessons.keyStatement: If the question is who has authority to decide, it is a door; if it is how the decision lands, it is yours to work.

items.title: Tribal consultation
items.body: Any action with Tribal implications goes to the DHS consultation process. It is not satisfied by a survey, a listening session or a county intermediary.

items.title: Rates and procurement
items.body: Rate methodology changes follow the rates and legislative process. Contract terms are set through procurement. Units propose; these offices decide.

items.title: Eligibility and licensing
items.body: Who qualifies, how assessments are done and what a 245D license requires are set by policy and licensing processes, not adjusted locally for convenience.

items.title: EOAD, legal and maltreatment
items.body: Complaints of discrimination, questions of legal duty, and risk of harm to a vulnerable adult each have a required path. Route them the same day.

tabs.label: Only one provider
tabs.body: A county has one enrolled provider for a service and the person wants a different one. Judgment: how to document real choice and what outreach to new providers looks like. Door: any question about changing the authorization or eligibility.

tabs.label: Tribal program overlap
tabs.body: A Nation's own program delivers something like the waiver service. Judgment: how your guidance describes coordination. Door: whether the state rule applies on the reservation, which is consultation.

tabs.label: Rural rate complaint
tabs.body: Providers say the rate does not cover travel. Judgment: documenting the evidence and proposing a travel component. Door: changing the rate, which follows the rates process.

check.question: A policy unit learns that a planned guidance change will affect how a Tribal Nation's human services program coordinates with the waiver. A team member proposes inviting the Nation's director to the next stakeholder call. What is the right move?
check.correct: Route the matter to the DHS Tribal consultation process now and let the stakeholder call proceed on other items.
wrong: Invite the director to the stakeholder call and treat their input as consultation if they attend.
Proceed with the guidance and plan to consult if the Nation raises a concern later.
Ask the county lead agency to brief the Nation on the change.
check.feedbackCorrect: Consultation is government-to-government and has its own process. The stakeholder call is useful for other things but does not replace it.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An invitation, a later reaction or a county briefing are not consultation. Name the door and route it before the guidance moves.

items.text: Whether to add a recorded option to a required training.
Whether a new rule applies to services delivered on a reservation.
Whether the mileage cap in the rate should change.
How to phrase the response-time standard in a memo.
A provider says it was denied a contract because of where it is located and the owner's national origin.
How a guidance document describes coordination with a Nation's program.

lessons.next: Next, you apply the whole course to one live piece of work and see what changes.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Casey leads a cross-unit group reviewing a waiver service standard. Three issues surface in one meeting. A rural county reports that the required in-person frequency is unworkable. A Nation has asked how the standard interacts with its own program. A provider has complained that the current rate ignores travel. The group has an hour and wants to leave with a plan. Someone suggests solving all three in the room.
scenario.prompt: How should Casey run the hour?
options: Sort the three issues first: work the frequency wording in the room, route the Nation's question to consultation today, and prepare a rate proposal with evidence for the rates process.
Work all three in the room since the group has the expertise and the time.
Send all three to legal and wait for guidance before doing anything.
responses: Yes. One is judgment, one is a consultation door, one is a rates door. Sorting first means the group leaves with the right next step for each.
The group can draft good ideas on all three, but two of them are not the group's to decide. Working them in the room delays the real process.
Sending judgment calls to legal is not a plan. Route the two doors and work the one that is yours.

lessons.transfer: Think of a place problem your unit has discussed more than once without resolving. Was it a judgment call that needed a decision, or a door that needed routing? What would the one-sentence routing note say?

move.control: You control whether a place problem is sorted before it is discussed, and whether a door is named in the record.
move.failure: Teams keep workshopping consultation duties and rate changes, feel productive, and nothing reaches the office that can decide.
move.next: At the next unit meeting the lead sorts any open place issue into work-it or route-it and records the routing with an owner and a date.

lessons.title: Run It on Something Real
lessons.summary: Apply the place read to one live decision this week, repair what was missed, and review what changed.
lessons.objective: Complete a place read on a current piece of work and record one repair and one result.
takeaways: One real draft beats ten examples.
Repair is normal; a decision that already went out can still get a paper path or a check-in.
Review what changed, in the draft and in the review list, not just whether the read was done.
lessons.statement: The default: the course ends and the method stays in the course. The better practice: the method runs on one live object this week, and the result is visible to someone else.

image.caption: Two colleagues working a proposal; the draft can still change, and this is where the place read earns its hour.

intro.heading: One object, this week
intro.body:
Pick one current piece of work. A draft policy, a rate memo, a contract term, a training plan, a timeline, an engagement plan or a data report. It should be something that has not locked yet, or something that locked recently and can still be repaired. Run the place read on it. Map the places it touches. Test it from the hardest county. Ask someone from that setting and, if a Nation is affected, route it to consultation. Adjust and record.

Repair is part of the practice. If something already went out with a metro default in it, you can still add a paper path, a recorded option, a check-in date or a note to the rates team. A repair is not an admission of failure. It is the method working on something that was written before you had it.

Then review. Not whether the read was done, but what changed. Did a requirement get a hybrid option? Did a reader from outside the metro join the list? Did a report gain a by-place breakout? Did a Tribal question get routed? Write it in three lines and share it with your supervisor or team. This course prepares you for the fuller equity analysis of policy changes, grants and contracting, provider networks and implementation timelines. All of those start with the question you can now ask: where does this land?

inThisLesson: Choose one current piece of work and run the full place read on it.
Make one repair to a decision that already went out, if there is one.
Record what changed in three lines and share it.
Plan the next object and the next review date.
lessons.keyStatement: The method counts when it runs on a real draft and someone else can see what changed.

items.title: Not locked yet
items.body: A draft due in the next two to four weeks is ideal. The read changes it before sign-off, which is the point.

items.title: Recently locked
items.body: Something that went out in the last quarter and can still take a repair: a paper path, a recorded session, a check-in date.

items.title: A recurring report
items.body: A measure you report every cycle. Adding a by-place breakout is a repair that keeps paying.

items.title: Not a whole program
items.body: Keep it to one object. The point is to finish the read and see a change, not to redesign a service in a week.

tabs.label: What changed
tabs.body: One sentence on the adjustment: the requirement that gained an option, the reader who joined, the breakout that was added.

tabs.label: What was routed
tabs.body: One sentence naming any door that opened: consultation, rates, procurement, eligibility, EOAD, with the date it was sent.

tabs.label: What is next
tabs.body: One sentence with the next object, its owner and the date you will look at it again.

check.question: A supervisor finishes the place read on a training plan and finds that the only change needed is adding a recorded option. The supervisor feels the read was not worth the time. What is the best way to think about this?
check.correct: A small change that reaches providers who would otherwise have been left out is the method working; record it and run the read on the next object.
wrong: The read is only useful for large decisions and should be reserved for those.
The read should be repeated with a harder county until it finds a bigger problem.
Skip recording it since the change was minor.
check.feedbackCorrect: Small, specific adjustments are the usual result. The habit is what matters, and the record makes it visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Judge the read by who it reached, not by the size of the change. Record it and keep the habit going.

items.text: Test the draft from the county with two enrolled providers.
Add a phone route to a form that went out online-only last month.
Write three lines on what changed and share them with the team.
Name the Nations affected by the draft.
Set a sixty-day check-in on a timeline that already started.
Confirm a rural reader actually joined the standing list.

lessons.next: Open the job aid, pick your object, and run the read this week; the courses on policy analysis, grants and contracting, provider networks and implementation timelines pick up where this ends.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Dana supervises a small policy team. Two weeks ago the team sent out guidance with an online-only acknowledgment form and a single metro listening session. A rural lead agency has now written to say three of its providers cannot complete the form. Dana's team is already busy with the next draft and someone suggests handling the rural request as an exception and moving on. Dana has the job aid open.
scenario.prompt: What should Dana do with the guidance that already went out?
options: Grant the exception for those three providers and note it in the file.
Withdraw the guidance and reissue it after a full place read.
Repair it now: add a paper and phone route for everyone, schedule a remote session, record the repair, and run the place read on the next draft before it goes out.
responses: An exception fixes three providers and leaves the default in place for everyone else who did not write in.
Withdrawal is rarely needed. The guidance is sound; the access paths are what failed, and those can be added.
This is the practice. Repair the paths for everyone, record it, and let the next draft benefit from the read before it locks.

lessons.transfer: What is the one object you will run the read on this week, and who will you show the three-line record to? If nothing on your desk qualifies, what recent decision could still take a repair?

move.control: You control which object gets the read this week and whether the three-line record is shared.
move.failure: The course is completed, the job aid is saved, and no draft changes.
move.next: By the end of this week the learner runs the read on one object, records three lines, and reviews them with their supervisor on a date set now.

jobAid.subtitle: Map. Test. Ask. Adjust. Route the doors.
remember: Identical is not equal; read every draft for where it lands.
Test against the hardest county, not the typical one.
Tribal effects go to consultation, not to a survey.

sections.heading: Map the places
items: List the counties with the fewest enrolled providers for this service.
Name the Tribal Nations whose members or programs the decision affects.
If you do not know either, record that as the first finding and find out.

sections.heading: Test from the hardest county
items: Read each requirement as a provider, a worker and a person in that county.
Write the cost in travel, broadband, provider choice and transit.
Flag any sentence that names no place but lands differently by place.

sections.heading: Ask the right people
items: Reach one reader from the hardest setting before the draft is final.
Route anything with Tribal implications to the DHS Tribal consultation process and hold the draft.
Add a rural and a Tribal area reader to the standing list for this document type.

sections.heading: Adjust and record
items: Add hybrid or recorded options, a travel component, a longer window or a paper path where the cost was high.
Record what changed, what did not and why, on one page attached to the draft.
Break out any related measure by county and Tribal area in the next report.

sections.heading: Route the doors
items: Rate changes go to the rates process; contract terms go to procurement.
Eligibility, assessment and licensing questions go to their policy offices.
Discrimination concerns go to EOAD or MDHR; risk of harm to a vulnerable adult is reported the same day.
Write the one-sentence routing note with an owner and a date.
